opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly my answer has shifted a lot over the last few years.

If you'd asked me five or six years ago, I would have said the gap was enormous and kind of unknowable. Back then, every robot learning project was its own little island: you'd collect data for one task, in one lab, on one robot, and you'd be thrilled if you got a policy that could open a specific drawer eighty percent of the time. There was no clear path from that to anything general.

What's changed is that we now have a recipe that seems to scale. Foundation models trained on internet-scale data gave robots something they never had before: common sense, semantic understanding, the ability to take an open-ended instruction and reason about it. When we started plugging vision-language models into robot policies, we saw that the robot could do things it was never explicitly trained on. It could pick up "the extinct animal" and grab the toy dinosaur, because that knowledge came from the web, not from robot data. That was a real moment for a lot of us. It suggested the high-level reasoning part of the problem might get largely inherited from progress elsewhere in AI.

So where's the gap now? I'd break it into a few pieces.

The first is physical dexterity and low-level control. Reasoning about what to do is increasingly tractable. Actually doing it with the precision, robustness, and contact-rich finesse a human has is still really hard. Folding laundry, handling deformable objects, using tools, recovering when something slips: we've seen impressive demos, but reliability over long horizons in messy environments is not where it needs to be.

The second is data. Language models had the whole internet. Robotics doesn't have an equivalent corpus of physical interaction data. Efforts like Open X-Embodiment, where many labs pooled data across lots of robot types, showed that cross-embodiment transfer actually works and that more diverse data helps. But we're still orders of magnitude short of where the language world was. A lot of the field's energy now goes into closing that gap through teleoperation at scale, simulation, learning from human video, and eventually robots generating their own data once deployed.

The third is evaluation and reliability. In language, a model that's right ninety percent of the time is useful. In the physical world, a ten percent failure rate might mean broken dishes or something unsafe. Getting the long tail of reliability, and even measuring progress in a reproducible way across labs, is an underappreciated bottleneck.

So my overall assessment: the conceptual gap has narrowed a lot. I don't think we're missing some fundamental idea the way we arguably were before. It feels more like an engineering and scaling problem now, which is exciting, because those tend to yield to sustained effort and resources. But the practical gap, getting from impressive lab demos to robots that work reliably in your home on day one, is still substantial. I'd be surprised if it closed as fast as the most bullish takes suggest, but I'd also be surprised if it took as long as skeptics expect. The trajectory has bent in a way that's hard to ignore.

r001.rationale: The response says the conceptual gap has narrowed and describes reliability and engineering challenges, but it does not distinguish readiness for commercially useful applications from whether further research breakthroughs are needed for full embodied AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the gap is still large, but it's a different kind of gap than it was even three or four years ago, and that distinction matters.

If you'd asked me in 2020, the gap was basically everywhere. We didn't have models that could understand natural language instructions in an open-ended way, we didn't have good visual representations that transferred across environments, and the policies we trained were brittle in the sense that a slightly different lighting condition or a new object would break them. So the problem felt like a long list of unsolved research problems that all had to be cracked independently.

What's changed is that the foundation model wave has essentially given us the "brain" part for free, or at least much cheaper than we expected. Vision-language models can look at a scene and tell you what's in it, reason about what needs to happen, break a task into steps, and even handle surprisingly out-of-distribution situations. That high-level semantic understanding used to be considered one of the hardest parts of robotics, and now it's arguably the most mature part of the stack.

So the gap has concentrated. It's now very much about the last mile between understanding and action. Can the system actually execute a dexterous, contact-rich manipulation reliably, hundreds of times in a row, in a kitchen it's never seen? Can it recover gracefully when something slips? Can it do this at a speed and cost that makes it useful rather than a demo? That's where things still fall apart. The demo-to-deployment ratio in robotics is brutal. A 70 percent success rate looks great in a video and is completely unusable as a product.

The other big piece is data. Language models got to ride on the internet. There's no internet of robot experience. Every approach, whether it's teleoperation at scale, simulation, learning from human video, or cross-embodiment transfer, is really a bet on how to manufacture that data flywheel. I don't think any of them has clearly won yet, and I think the field is still underestimating how much data it will actually take to get to true generality.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: we've closed most of the gap on knowing what to do, and we've closed much less of it on actually doing it robustly in the physical world. The optimistic read is that the remaining problems are more legible than they used to be. The sober read is that legible doesn't mean easy, and the physical world is a very unforgiving teacher.

r001.rationale: The response describes high-level semantic capabilities as relatively mature, while saying reliable, cost-effective physical execution remains inadequate for products and that the data needed for true generality is unresolved. This distinguishes current ingredient readiness from the remaining gap to embodied AGI.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s still a substantial gap, but it helps to separate two things: what a robot can do in a demonstration, and what it can reliably do when you put it in a new environment. You can have a robot perform a really impressive task, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it understands how to handle all the variations of that task, recognize when something has gone wrong, or recover without a person stepping in.

For me, the full vision of embodied AGI is much closer to being able to give a robot a goal and have it figure out how to accomplish that goal in a world it hasn’t seen before. That requires more than good motor control. It requires reasoning, learning from experience, and connecting those capabilities to physical action.

The exciting thing is that we’re starting to see ways to bring those pieces together. But I’d be cautious about equating an impressive demo with having solved the underlying problem. The question is how broadly the capability transfers, how reliably it works, and how much human support it needs. That’s where I think a lot of the remaining gap lives.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gap between impressive demonstrations and reliable transfer toward embodied AGI, but it does not communicate that current robotics ingredients are ready for commercially useful applications while further research breakthroughs are needed for full embodied AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s still a pretty substantial gap, but it helps to break down what we mean by that. If you look at a robot doing a particular task in a particular environment, you can get really impressive performance today. The harder question is: how much of that capability survives when you change the task, the objects, or the environment?

For me, the vision of embodied AGI is a system that can walk into a new situation, understand what needs to happen, and use its experience to figure out how to do it. It should also recognize when it doesn’t know something and learn from a small amount of interaction. We’re still far from having that whole package reliably.

One thing that makes robotics especially challenging is that you have to close the loop with the physical world. Having a reasonable plan is useful, but you also need to execute it, notice that something slipped or that an object wasn’t where you expected, and recover. Those details can determine whether a task actually succeeds.

So I’m excited by the progress toward more general policies and transferring knowledge across tasks. But I’d distinguish between a compelling demonstration and a robot you can leave operating independently for hours. Getting from one to the other requires much better generalization, reliability, and recovery. That’s a big part of the gap I think we still need to close.

r001.rationale: The response describes impressive performance on specific tasks and says full embodied AGI still needs better generalization, reliability, and recovery. It does not distinguish current robotics ingredients as ready for commercially useful applications, so the full criterion is not communicated.
